title: Weave Two Strings
statement:
You get three strings s1, s2 and s3. Decide whether s3 is a weave of the other two: you can build it by repeatedly taking the next unused character from either s1 or s2, until both are used up.

Every character of s1 and s2 must be used exactly once, and each string's own characters must appear in s3 in their original order. You may switch between the two strings as often as you like. Return true or false.

examples.why: Take "ac" from s2, then "ab" from s1. Grabbing the first a from s1 because it matches leads to a dead end, so choosing greedily fails.
s3 has 3 characters but the other two have only 2 together.
The letters are right, but b comes before a, which breaks the order of s1.

constraints: All strings hold lowercase English letters
hints: When the next character of s3 matches the next unused character of both s1 and s2, you cannot know which one to take. You have to be able to try both cheaply.
The state is just how many characters of s1 (i) and of s2 (j) you have used; together they have produced s3[0..i+j). Let dp[i][j] say whether that is possible.
The last character s3[i+j−1] came from s1 or from s2: dp[i][j] = (dp[i−1][j] and s1[i−1] == s3[i+j−1]) or (dp[i][j−1] and s2[j−1] == s3[i+j−1]), with dp[0][0] = true. Check the lengths first.

explain.intuition:
Picture s1 and s2 as two queues and s3 as the order in which you pull from them. A greedy rule ("take from s1 when it matches") fails when both queues offer the same letter, as in the first example. But the history does not matter, only how far each queue has been drained. That is two numbers, so the state space is a grid.

Let dp[i][j] be true when the first i characters of s1 and the first j of s2 can be woven into exactly s3[0..i+j). Read it off the last decision: the last character s3[i+j−1] was taken either from s1 (then it equals s1[i−1] and dp[i−1][j] must hold) or from s2 (it equals s2[j−1] and dp[i][j−1] must hold). Each cell needs only the cell above and the cell to the left, the same shape as counting grid routes, so one row is enough. In fact this is a grid walk: moving down uses a letter of s1, moving right uses one of s2, and you ask whether some route reaches the bottom-right corner.
steps: Let row have s2.length + 1 entries. Fill row 0: row[0] = true, and row[j] = row[j−1] and s2[j−1] == s3[j−1].
For each i from 1: row[0] = row[0] and s1[i−1] == s3[i−1]. Then for each j from 1: row[j] = (row[j] and s1[i−1] == s3[i+j−1]) or (row[j−1] and s2[j−1] == s3[i+j−1]).
The old row[j] is the cell above (took from s1); row[j−1] is the cell to the left, already updated (took from s2). Return row[s2.length].
pitfalls: Skipping the length check. The table only looks at the first n + m characters of s3, so s1 = "a", s2 = "b", s3 = "abb" would wrongly return true.
Choosing greedily, or trying s1 first and only trying s2 if s1 does not match. Both letters can match, and only one choice may work.
Only checking that the letter counts agree. The third example has the right letters in the wrong order.

solutions.title: Recursion over both choices
solutions.idea: From (i, j), if the next s3 character matches s1[i] try taking it, and if it matches s2[j] try that too. No memory, so long runs of equal letters explode.

solutions.title: Table over both prefixes
solutions.idea: dp[i][j]: can s1[0..i) and s2[0..j) weave into s3[0..i+j)? The last character came from s1 (cell above) or s2 (cell to the left).

solutions.title: One row
solutions.idea: Each cell reads the cell above (the old row[j]) and the cell to the left (row[j − 1], already updated), so one row is enough.

followups: Return which characters of s3 came from s1, not just true or false.
Weave three strings instead of two. How big is the state now?
Solve it with memoized recursion and compare how many states each version visits on a false input.
